case_study_insert.main_stem: Redwood Trail Express (RTE) is a partnership in the parcel delivery and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2015 by Priya Raman and Dan Okoro, it delivers e-commerce parcels for online retailers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. RTE plans to invest $450,000 in an automated parcel-sorting hub and electric delivery vans, financed by a $290,000 bank loan and $160,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $140,000 a year, a variable cost of $2.50 a unit and a selling price of $6.00, and currently handles 95,000 units a year. RTE faces an operational problem: parcel damage has reached 3.1% and absenteeism is rising, while its depot reports growing sorting errors during peak periods.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Depot Sorting and Market Report — Q3 2025: The hub sorted 24,000 parcels last quarter with a damage rate of 3.1%, down from 4.7% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 61 to 34 per month. Average delivery time is 2.4 days and sorting errors affected 2.6% of parcels. Van downtime is 5.3% of scheduled hours. Market research of 700 online shoppers found 66% would pay $0.40 more for a same-day parcel service, and 57% choose couriers on reliability. A review shows 16 of 55 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new sorters; off-the-job training at the local college is also an option. Managers are considering a bonus scheme and job rotation to cut sorting errors.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Redwood Trail Express for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.40 to $13.20 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across courier firms. (3) Fuel and packaging input costs have risen 8.8% year-on-year, transport inflation is 6.5%, and e-commerce parcel volumes grew 5.4%.

questions.question_text: RTE plans to fund part of its $450,000 sorting hub with $160,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for RTE of using retained profit instead of the $290,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest or instalments, which protects the cash flow of a 55-employee partnership already carrying fixed costs of $140,000 a year and a $290,000 bank loan. The savings can be spent on reducing the 3.1% parcel damage rate and the 2.6% sorting errors without raising the $6.00 selling price to online retailers. With the base rate rising to 4.75% (Appendix 3), internal funds avoid the dearer debt.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps control with founders Priya Raman and Dan Okoro, with no bank conditions attached to the $450,000 investment and no asset at risk of repossession if the new hub fails to cut the 5.3% van downtime. It is also faster to deploy than negotiating more debt, so the electric vans and sorters can be installed before the next peak period when sorting errors currently rise, protecting the 57% of shoppers who choose couriers on reliability.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to RTE and the case data.

questions.question_text: RTE is launching a same-day parcel service for online retailers. Consider a television campaign, sponsorship of retailer websites, or social media advertising. Which should RTE choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: TV could build fast, broad awareness of same-day delivery and support a $0.40 premium, but airtime is very expensive for a partnership funding a $450,000 hub, and most viewers are not the online retailers who place the 24,000 quarterly parcel orders. Much of the spend would be wasted.

Sponsorship of retailer websites: Placing the same-day message on the sites of the e-commerce retailers RTE already serves reaches shoppers exactly at the point of purchase, lending credibility and directly supporting the 66% of 700 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.40 more. It is cheaper than television and measurable. Its limits are dependence on retailer agreements and narrower reach than mass media, so it may not rapidly build the brand needed to win new retail accounts.

Social media advertising: Targeted social ads can reach online shoppers by interest at low cost, and parcel volume grew 5.4%, so demand is rising. The audience is broad rather than trade-specific and results depend on constant optimisation, but it is flexible and scalable.

Recommendation: RTE should choose sponsorship of retailer websites. It reaches buyers at the moment they choose a courier and reinforces the reliability that 57% of shoppers value, with far less waste than television and more trade relevance than general social ads. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and social media is rejected as less direct at the point of sale; RTE can add retargeting later.

Sponsorship also lets RTE link the same-day message to the 2.4-day average delivery time and the falling 3.1% damage rate, giving retailers concrete evidence of reliability before they commit to the $0.40 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to RTE's retailers.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with RTE context and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of RTE's survey data and parcel volumes, with a justified recommendation explaining why television and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: RTE's 3.1% parcel damage rate and rising absenteeism are hurting service. Explain two benefits for RTE of introducing team working in the sorting hub.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working makes the 55 staff jointly responsible for load quality, so peers can spot and prevent the 3.1% parcel damage and the 2.6% sorting errors before parcels leave the hub. Shared monitoring is especially valuable under laissez-faire leadership, where supervision is light, and it protects the $6.00 price and the 66% of shoppers willing to pay $0.40 more for reliable same-day delivery.

Point 2: Teams reduce the isolation of depot work and give staff social support, which can improve morale and curb the rising absenteeism that currently pushes up 5.3% van downtime. Members can cover for absent colleagues and share skills learned on the new sorters, so the 24,000 parcels handled each quarter are maintained while the $450,000 hub beds in and the damage rate falls towards the 4.7% benchmark of a year ago.

Teams can also share feedback from the 34 monthly complaints still received, turning service failures into practical improvements and helping the partnership protect the 66% of shoppers willing to pay $0.40 more for a reliable same-day parcel service.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to RTE and the case data.

questions.question_text: RTE wants to cut sorting errors and damage. Consider a performance-related bonus or job rotation. Which should RTE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonus: Paying a bonus for error-free sorting would motivate the 55 staff financially and could quickly reduce the 3.1% damage rate and 2.6% sorting errors, raising output from the 24,000 parcels handled each quarter. However, a speed-linked bonus might encourage rushed handling and actually increase damage, it adds to wage costs when the minimum wage is rising 5.5%, and it does nothing to cover for the rising absenteeism.

Job rotation: Moving staff between sorting, loading and van duties builds a multi-skilled workforce that can cover absent colleagues and reduce the 5.3% van downtime. It also reduces the boredom that drives errors during peak periods, tackling the 2.6% sorting-error rate at its source. The drawbacks are slower initial output while staff learn each task and the need for more on-the-job training on the new sorters, which takes time away from the $450,000 hub's throughput.

Decision: RTE should choose job rotation. It addresses both the 2.6% sorting errors and the rising absenteeism by creating flexible, engaged staff, and it avoids the perverse incentive of a bonus that could worsen the 3.1% damage rate. The bonus is rejected because it adds cost while wages rise 5.5% and does not solve the coverage problem; RTE can add a small quality bonus once error rates are stable.

To make rotation work, RTE can pair each driver with an experienced colleague for the first few shifts, keeping the 24,000 quarterly parcels moving while skills transfer. It should also monitor the 3.1% damage rate weekly so that any quality dip caused by learning is caught before it affects the 66% of shoppers willing to pay the $0.40 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two HR options with little application to RTE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of both options in RTE's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensively evaluates both options against cost, quality and absence, with a clear decision and explicit reasons for rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RTE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $140,000 ÷ ($6.00 − $2.50) = $140,000 ÷ $3.50 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 parcels a year.
Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 95,000 − 40,000 = 55,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 55,000 parcels a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RTE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. A margin of safety of 55,000 parcels against 95,000 actual shows the hub can lose a large share of e-commerce volume before breaking even.
2. Contribution of $3.50 a parcel ($6.00 − $2.50) lets managers model the $0.40 same-day premium and judge whether discounts to online retailers are affordable.
3. Knowing break-even of 40,000 helps test whether the $290,000 bank loan can be serviced before adding more electric vans to the $450,000 investment.
4. Monitoring unit cost against the 8.8% fuel and packaging rise and the 5.3% van downtime helps target waste reduction and protect the 57% of shoppers who value reliability.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Margin of safety = 55,000 parcels | (iii) Four contextual uses: cushion of 55,000 parcels; modelling the $0.40 same-day premium on $3.50 contribution; servicing the $290,000 loan; and controlling 8.8% input inflation and 5.3% van downtime.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RTE's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has RTE's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 35.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $540,000 ÷ revenue $1,800,000 × 100 = 30.0; 2025 $735,000 ÷ $2,100,000 × 100 = 35.0. Operating profit $270,000 ÷ revenue $1,800,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2024 and $378,000 ÷ $2,100,000 × 100 = 18.0 in 2025. Returns on capital: $270,000 ÷ $1,500,000 × 100 = 18.0 in 2024 and $378,000 ÷ $1,800,000 × 100 = 21.0 in 2025. Cost of sales rose from $1,260,000 to $1,365,000 while revenue grew $300,000, so gross profit increased by $195,000. Interest payable fell from $18,000 to $15,000.

Evaluation: All three measures moved upwards. The gross margin improved from 30.0% to 35.0%, showing better control of direct parcel costs despite the 8.8% fuel and packaging rise. The operating margin rose from 15.0% to 18.0%, so more of each revenue dollar survives the $140,000 fixed costs. Returns on capital increased from 18.0% to 21.0%, meaning the $1,800,000 capital employed is generating more profit. These are real gains because revenue and gross profit both grew. The concern is that damage is still 3.1% and van downtime 5.3%, which could raise costs and reverse the improvement if the $450,000 hub is poorly managed.

Conclusion: RTE's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (30.0% to 35.0%), operating margin (15.0% to 18.0%) and returns on capital (18.0% to 21.0%) all rose together on the back of higher revenue and gross profit. RTE should defend the gain by using retained profit to cut the 3.1% damage rate and 5.3% downtime.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RTE of switching its fleet to electric delivery vans.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Electric vans reduce exposure to the 8.8% rise in fuel and packaging input costs and cut the 5.3% downtime associated with older vehicles, protecting the $2.50 variable cost and the $3.50 contribution on each of the 95,000 parcels. A greener fleet also strengthens the reliability and sustainability message to the 57% of shoppers who choose couriers on reliability and supports the $450,000 hub investment.

Disadvantage: The vans form part of the $450,000 outlay funded by a $290,000 bank loan while the base rate rises to 4.75%, so cash flow may be tight if parcel volumes grow more slowly than the 5.4% forecast. Charging and new-vehicle maintenance also need staff trained on the new sorters and vans, difficult while absenteeism is rising and the 3.1% damage rate and 2.6% sorting errors already strain peak-period operations.

Charging schedules can be planned around the 2.4-day average delivery time, and lower running costs would protect the $3.50 contribution per parcel as e-commerce volumes grow only 5.4% and the 5.3% van downtime is reduced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to RTE and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.8% rise in fuel and packaging input costs will affect RTE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (4.0% to 4.75%): If RTE's $290,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $290,000 = $2,175 a year (0.0075 × $290,000). That is small against fixed costs of $140,000 a year, and zero if the loan is fixed. Higher rates could make online retailers cautious and raise future borrowing costs for the $450,000 hub, but the direct interest effect is limited.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.20 an hour): With a workforce of 55 in sorting and driving, this lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay are given, so an annual total cannot be invented; the sound comparison is productivity, 95,000 parcels ÷ 55 staff = about 1,727 parcels per worker. If that holds, the rise is manageable; if rising absenteeism cuts it, unit labour cost rises and the $3.50 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation (8.8% fuel and packaging): The $2.50 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole $2.50 rose 8.8%, that adds 8.8% × $2.50 = $0.22 a parcel; across 95,000 parcels a year that is about $20,900 (95,000 × $0.22). That would reduce contribution from $3.50 to about $3.28 on every parcel and compounds on the existing 5.3% van downtime. Part can be recovered through the $0.40 same-day premium.

Conclusion: The 8.8% rise in fuel and packaging input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 95,000 parcels and erodes the $3.50 contribution that supports the $450,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $2,175 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity holds. RTE should cut van downtime and waste first.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to RTE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on RTE's costs, revenue or financing in context, using insert figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in RTE's context with a well-justified judgement that input cost inflation has the greatest impact and clear reasons why the other two are smaller.
